title: Set Compatibility
description: Align SQL set operands by column count, position, type and meaning, with explicit duplicate, NULL, provenance, collation and ordering policies.
notes:
## Align meaning before combining query results

Set operations combine the rows produced by separate queries. For the combination to be useful, each operand must describe compatible columns in the same positions. The engine can check some structural and type requirements, but it cannot establish that the values represent the same business concept. Combining student identifiers with room numbers may be syntactically acceptable while producing a result with no coherent interpretation.

Study [UNION](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-sql), [UNION ALL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-all), [INTERSECT](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/intersect) and [EXCEPT](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/except) alongside this topic. MySQL 8.4 supports these set operations. Their combination rules include positional compatibility, result-type derivation and duplicate semantics. Other engines and older versions can have different support and conversion details.

## Match the number of projected columns

Every operand in a set operation must project the same number of columns. A two-column query cannot be unioned directly with a one-column query merely because they share one alias. Decide the intended output schema, then explicitly project each operand into that shape. Avoid SELECT * because a later source-table change can alter the arity or positional meaning unexpectedly.

```sql
SELECT learner_id, display_name FROM morning_roster
UNION ALL
SELECT learner_id, display_name FROM evening_roster;
```

Both operands here provide an identifier followed by a name. The source tables may contain other fields in different storage orders without affecting this explicit projection. A schema-compatible projection creates a clear review boundary: the combined output has exactly the columns the consumer expects rather than whatever happens to exist in each table today.

## Align by position rather than by alias

Set operands are paired by column position. The first expression of the second operand aligns with the first expression of the first operand, even if their aliases are different or misleading. Naming the second query's first expression display_name does not tell the engine to search for a matching alias elsewhere in the first query.

A dangerous example reverses identifier and name positions in the second operand. Depending on type-conversion rules, the query may fail or coerce values into a broader result type. Neither outcome should be relied on as semantic validation. Write both projections in a visibly parallel order and review each position against the intended output definition.

## Check compatible types without relying on accidental coercion

MySQL derives a result type that accounts for corresponding expressions. This can widen representations and change how values are delivered to a client. An integer-like identifier combined with textual identifiers may no longer arrive in the same type a caller expected. Explicit casts can document the desired shared representation when the values truly belong to the same domain.

Casts do not make unrelated domains meaningful. A course code and a building code remain different concepts after both are cast to text. Likewise, amounts denominated in different currencies are not comparable merely because they share DECIMAL. Establish units and identity domains before choosing a conversion, and preserve a source or currency label when that distinction belongs in the output.

## Use typed placeholders for genuinely absent fields

One source may lack an attribute that the combined output intentionally permits to be unknown. A projected null can represent that absence. An explicit cast on the placeholder can make the intended output type clear. An empty string or numeric zero is a different value and should not be used as a universal substitute for unavailable information.

```sql
SELECT learner_id, CAST(NULL AS CHAR(20)) AS cohort_label
FROM legacy_roster
UNION ALL
SELECT learner_id, cohort_label
FROM current_roster;
```

This design needs a stated contract: the missing legacy cohort is unknown, not necessarily an empty label or an unassigned current cohort. If consumers need to distinguish those states, add a source or provenance field. A technically compatible two-column result can still erase information when absent values are flattened into one ambiguous presentation.

## Decide what makes rows duplicates

UNION removes duplicate result rows by default, while UNION ALL retains their appearances. Duplicate comparison concerns the complete projected row, not a hidden source identity. If two learners share a name and the projection contains only that name, UNION can merge their labels even though the underlying people are distinct. Include the identity when the task concerns distinct learners.

Adding a source label changes duplicate semantics because it becomes another projected value. Two otherwise equal rows labeled morning and evening are now distinct full rows. That can be exactly what an attendance-source report needs. It is not equivalent to a deduplicated learner list, so choose provenance columns according to the requested grain rather than adding or removing them casually.

## Treat NULL duplicate behavior separately from equality predicates

Set duplicate handling can treat two null-bearing result rows as duplicates even though a WHERE equality comparison involving null is unknown. Do not transfer the truth table of a row predicate directly to the set operator's duplicate-elimination rules. In a fixture with two identical unknown cohort rows, UNION can retain one appearance where UNION ALL retains both.

This behavior also matters for INTERSECT and EXCEPT when null-bearing rows appear in both operands. Clarify whether the desired result is set-oriented or multiplicity-oriented, and use supported ALL forms where the task requires them. A null placeholder inserted for compatibility participates in the complete row comparison, so its meaning should be reviewed before deduplication.

## Account for text comparison rules

Character set and collation influence which text values can be combined and how comparisons treat case or accents. A report that assumes differently cased learner codes are distinct may behave differently under a case-insensitive collation. Conversely, incompatible collations can require an explicit consistent choice rather than a guessed conversion.

Do not change database-wide collation just to make one teaching query run. Identify the column or expression contract and use a suitable local expression when authorized. If text codes are identities, define their comparison semantics at the system boundary. A lesson's sample ASCII names cannot establish how every international name or code behaves.

## Apply final sorting to the combined relation

The final ORDER BY belongs to the combined result when the task asks for global order. Sorting one operand does not establish the order of all rows after a set operation. Refer to the result's visible column names or another supported ordering form, and use unambiguous aliases in the first projection for a clear consumer-facing schema.

Parentheses matter when mixing operators, limits or operand-specific ordering. MySQL gives INTERSECT different precedence from UNION and EXCEPT, so use parentheses when the intended grouping could be misunderstood. The compatibility checks apply at each combination point. A three-query expression must have both a valid schema and the intended grouping of set operations.

## Review output contracts with contrasting fixtures

The exercises combine morning and evening rosters that share one exact learner row. UNION ALL retains both appearances, while UNION keeps one identical full row. Another learner shares a display name but has a different identifier, so that person must remain a separate row. The fixtures make projection and duplicate policy observable without relying on execution order.

When moving a combined result into an application, check column names, nullability and result types as well as row counts. Keep tenant and visibility restrictions within each operand so another source does not accidentally broaden access. Compatible SQL shape is the beginning of a correct set operation; compatible meaning, provenance and consumer expectations complete the definition.

## Design a common projection before touching the operator

Write a short output contract that assigns one meaning to each ordinal position: learner identity first, display label second, and source third only if source belongs to the requested grain. Then check both operands against that contract. This makes an accidental reversal visible before runtime conversion rules can disguise it.

If two sources disagree about the representation of the same identity, resolve that disagreement explicitly. Leading zeros can be meaningful in a textual code, while converting the code to a number can erase them. A successful cast only proves that conversion was possible for the supplied values. It does not prove that the resulting identity still means what downstream callers expect.

questions.question_text: How are columns aligned across set operands?
questions.explanation: The first expression aligns with the first expression regardless of labels.

questions.question_text: What arity must operands have?
options: The same number of projected columns
questions.explanation: Set operators require corresponding positions across operand projections.

questions.question_text: Why avoid SELECT* for a stable combined output?
options: Source changes can alter position and arity
questions.explanation: Explicit projections preserve the intended output schema.

questions.question_text: Does casting course codes and room codes to text establish a shared domain?
questions.explanation: Representation compatibility does not establish business meaning.

questions.question_text: What does UNION ALL retain?
questions.explanation: ALL preserves duplicate result appearances.

questions.question_text: What does ordinary UNION remove?
options: Every repeated name regardless of other columns
questions.explanation: Duplicate comparison concerns the full output row.

questions.question_text: Can projecting only names merge distinct people under UNION?
questions.explanation: Two identities sharing the same projected label can become one result row.

questions.question_text: What does a source label do to duplicate comparison?
options: It becomes another compared output value
It enforces one row per learner
questions.explanation: Different provenance labels make otherwise equal full rows distinct.

questions.question_text: What is a null placeholder suitable for?
options: Every absent value as measured zero
questions.explanation: NULL represents unknown information rather than an invented known value.

questions.question_text: Why cast a null placeholder explicitly?
options: To turn it into a real cohort
To document its intended shared type
questions.explanation: Typed expressions clarify the combined result representation.

questions.question_text: Are empty string and NULL interchangeable?
questions.explanation: An empty known string differs from unknown information.

questions.question_text: Can set deduplication treat two null-bearing equal rows as duplicates?
questions.explanation: Duplicate-elimination semantics differ from ordinary predicate equality.

questions.question_text: What can text collation affect?
questions.explanation: Collation controls how compatible text values are compared.

questions.question_text: Does sorting one operand guarantee global output order?
questions.explanation: The final combined relation needs its own requested order.

questions.question_text: Where should global ORDER BY apply?
options: Only to the first table scan
questions.explanation: Final ordering is defined after the set combination.

questions.question_text: Why parenthesize mixed set operators?
questions.explanation: Operator precedence can otherwise combine inputs in an unintended order.

questions.question_text: Does a numeric type prove compatible currency units?
questions.explanation: Currency meaning must be retained or converted by an explicit policy.

questions.question_text: What should client verification include besides rows?
questions.explanation: A combined result can change representation even when values look plausible.

questions.question_text: Where must access restrictions remain?
questions.explanation: Each source population must be authorized before its rows enter the result.

questions.question_text: Which fixture distinguishes identities from labels?
options: Different learner IDs sharing a name
questions.explanation: Keeping the identity prevents accidental merging of different people.

coding_problems.title: Combine roster appearances
coding_problems.task: Return learner_id,display_name from both rosters retaining all appearances. Order by learner_id,display_name.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE morning_roster(learner_id INT NOT NULL,display_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE evening_roster(learner_id INT NOT NULL,display_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO morning_roster VALUES (1,'Ari'),(2,'Bo'); INSERT INTO evening_roster VALUES (1,'Ari'),(3,'Bo');
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT learner_id,display_name FROM morning_roster UNION ALL SELECT learner_id,display_name FROM evening_roster ORDER BY learner_id,display_name;
coding_problems.expected:
learner_id	display_name
1	Ari
1	Ari
2	Bo
3	Bo

original_questions.question_text: What does set (union) compatibility require of two queries combined with UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT?
options: The same number of columns, with compatible types in corresponding positions
Both queries must reference the same table
Both queries must return the same number of rows
original_questions.explanation: Column count and type compatibility are the structural requirements — not matching names.

original_questions.question_text: Do the column names in the two queries combined by UNION need to match?
options: No — only column count and type compatibility matter; names don't need to match
Only the first column's name must match
Names must be different, never the same
original_questions.explanation: Structural compatibility is about count/type, not naming.

original_questions.question_text: Where do the final output column names in a UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT result come from?
options: Always auto-generated as col1, col2, etc.
original_questions.explanation: The first query's naming determines the combined result's output names.

original_questions.question_text: Is passing the set-compatibility check (right column count/types) a guarantee that the combination is semantically meaningful?
options: Yes, structural compatibility guarantees semantic correctness
No — the database only checks structure, not whether combining the data actually makes sense for the use case
Semantic meaning is checked automatically by every SQL engine
This distinction doesn't apply to set operations
original_questions.explanation: Structural compatibility and semantic sensibility are separate concerns — SQL only enforces the former.

original_questions.question_text: What happens if two queries combined with UNION have a different number of columns?
options: This is a hard error — column counts must match
Missing columns are automatically filled with NULL
The queries run separately and results are concatenated
original_questions.explanation: Mismatched column counts are a straightforward structural error, not silently resolved.

original_questions.question_text: Can an INT column and a DECIMAL column generally be combined via UNION?
options: Never, this always causes an error
Often yes, via implicit type conversion, though genuinely incompatible types (like numbers and non-numeric text) may error or convert unpredictably
Only if both columns contain exactly the same values
original_questions.explanation: Reasonably compatible numeric types are often implicitly converted, unlike fundamentally mismatched types.

original_questions.question_text: When is set compatibility checked relative to row-level operations like deduplication?
options: Before any row-level comparison — a structural mismatch is caught immediately regardless of the data
Only if ORDER BY is present
original_questions.explanation: Structural validation happens first, independent of the actual row data.

original_questions.question_text: Does set compatibility apply equally to UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT?
options: Yes — all three set operations share the same union-compatibility requirement
Set compatibility is unrelated to any of these operations
original_questions.explanation: The structural requirement is uniform across all set operations covered in this chapter.
